string.text: Pripyat Construction Brief

OFFICIAL BRIEF
Subject: the city of Pripyat, Kyiv Region.
Purpose: housing for employees of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant and their families.
 
Construction was authorized on February 4, 1970. Residential districts are to enter service together with schools, childcare facilities, shops, and cultural venues.
 
Average annual population growth exceeds 1,500: approximately 800 newborns and 500–600 specialists arriving for permanent employment.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The city is designed to expand alongside the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.%c[0,170,170,170]
Anniversary Events Plan

EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE OF THE PRIPYAT CITY COUNCIL
Events planned for spring 1986.
 
1. Prepare festive street decorations.
2. Hold sporting events and performances by local ensembles.
3. Complete improvements to the new residential areas.
4. Prepare recreational facilities for the summer season.
 
For reference: February 4 marked sixteen years since the decision to build Pripyat.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Clerk's note: implementation suspended following the evacuation of the city on April 27, 1986.%c[0,170,170,170]
TG-8 Test Log

UNIT 4. OPERATING LOG
Date: April 26, 1986.
Purpose: test whether turbine-generator rundown can power the pumps after loss of external electricity.
 
01:23:04 — test begins. Four main circulation pumps transferred to power from TG-8 rundown.
Water flow is falling. Steam content is rising.
01:23:40 — emergency shutdown initiated.
01:23:43 — sharp power surge registered. Explosions follow.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Condition: reactor and structural elements of the unit destroyed.%c[0,170,170,170]
Findings on the AZ-5 System

TECHNICAL FINDINGS
Subject: operation of the RBMK-1000 control and protection rods.
 
Under certain core conditions, the graphite displacers initially increase reactivity in the lower part of the core as the rods descend. Full insertion takes approximately eighteen seconds.
 
The operating documentation available to the shift did not disclose the possibility of a positive reactivity effect during shutdown. Dangerous behavior had previously been observed in other RBMK reactors.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Conclusion: pressing AZ-5 may have caused a brief increase in reactor power.%c[0,170,170,170]
Valery Khodemchuk's Personnel Card

PERSONNEL RECORD
Khodemchuk, Valery Ilyich. Born March 24, 1951.
Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant: employed since September 4, 1973.
Position: senior operator of the main circulation pumps, Unit 4.
 
On April 26, 1986, he was at his post in the northern pump hall. The room was destroyed by the first explosion. Searches through the surviving passages found nothing. Further access was halted by structural collapse and radiation conditions.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Status: deceased. Body not recovered; place of burial — the structure of Unit 4.%c[0,170,170,170]
Report on Vladimir Shashenok

ACCIDENT REPORT
Shashenok, Vladimir Nikolaevich, commissioning engineer for Smolenskatomenergonaladka.
 
Assigned to Unit 4 to take part in the test. At the time of the accident, he was monitoring system and equipment readings in the deaerator building.
 
He suffered multiple injuries and burns when the structure collapsed. Plant workers carried him from the room, and he was taken to the Pripyat medical center.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Physician's note: died of his injuries on April 26, 1986.%c[0,170,170,170]
Emergency Work Log: Turbine Hall

DRAFT SHIFT-ACTION LOG
Location: turbine hall shared by Units 3 and 4.
 
K. G. Perchuk — attempted to isolate a pump connected to a ruptured pipe; shut off the oil line.
A. I. Baranov — changed the turbine-generators from hydrogen to nitrogen to prevent another fire and explosion.
A. Kh. Kurguz — closed a sealed door; led personnel out of smoke-filled rooms.
 
Conditions: structural damage, steam, spilled oil, no lighting, and high radiation.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Result: the fire's spread through the turbine hall was contained.%c[0,170,170,170]
Fire Brigade Dispatch Log

FIRE SERVICE OPERATIONS LOG
April 26, 1986.
 
01:28 — the VPH-2 watch arrives at the accident site under Lieutenant Vladimir Pravik.
01:35 — the SVPH-6 watch from Pripyat arrives.
Assignment: extinguish the turbine-hall roof and fires near Unit 4; protect the adjacent unit.
 
The crews have no radiation protection designed for the actual exposure levels. Pravik, Kibenok, Ignatenko, Vashchuk, Tishura, and Titenok receive severe doses.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Note: all six died in May 1986 at Moscow Hospital No. 6.%c[0,170,170,170]
Radiation Report. Not for Release

PRIPYAT CITY REPORT
April 26–27, 1986.
 
Continuous monitoring of radiation conditions began on the morning of April 26. By evening, readings of hundreds of milliroentgens per hour had been recorded in parts of the city. Preparations began for transport and reception areas for the population.
 
Public announcement on April 26: none. The first city-radio announcement was made around noon on April 27. Wording: “temporary evacuation.”
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Time between the accident and notification of the public: approximately thirty-six hours.%c[0,170,170,170]
Pripyat Evacuation Register

TRANSPORT AND BOARDING REGISTER
Date: April 27, 1986.
 
Dispatched to the city: approximately 1,390 buses and three trains.
Boarding begins: 14:00.
Main operation completed: approximately 17:00.
Evacuated that day: approximately 45,000 people.
 
Permit documents, money, food for the first few days, and a minimum of personal belongings. Apartments are to be locked. Electrical appliances switched off. Gas and water shut off.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Public announcement: the evacuation is temporary; no return date is given.%c[0,170,170,170]
Instructions for Evacuees
Forsmark Station Log

TRANSLATED DUTY LOG. SWEDEN
Forsmark Nuclear Power Plant, April 28, 1986.
 
Morning — radiation monitors activate when workers enter from outdoors. Contamination found on footwear and clothing.
Ventilation, plant rooms, and emissions checked. No leak found at this facility.
Elevated activity detected on the ground. Air-mass analysis points to a source outside Sweden.
10:00 — findings forwarded to the Radiation Protection Institute.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Preliminary conclusion: accident at a nuclear facility in the western Soviet Union.%c[0,170,170,170]
May Day Demonstration Plan

KYIV CITY EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE
Event: May Day workers' demonstration, May 1, 1986.
 
Location: Central Square and Khreshchatyk.
Ensure the procession of columns, festive decorations, radio coverage, and maintenance of public order. Information about the accident at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant is not to be included in the holiday program.
 
For reference: by the date of the event, Pripyat has been evacuated, the government commission is working at the plant, and radioactive contamination has been detected outside the Soviet Union.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Decision: the demonstration will proceed according to the approved plan.%c[0,170,170,170]
Bubbler Pool Drainage Report

WORK COMPLETION REPORT
Site: rooms beneath the reactor, Unit 4.
 
Assignment: open the isolation valves and allow water to drain from the bubbler pool.
Personnel: mechanical engineer Alexei Ananenko, turbine-shop engineer Valery Bespalov, and shift supervisor Boris Baranov.
 
Ananenko and Bespalov located the valves. Baranov provided lighting and accompanied them. The valves were opened, and the remaining water was later pumped out.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]All personnel emerged alive. Reports that the team died during the mission are false.%c[0,170,170,170]
Army Aviation Flight Summary

HELICOPTER UNIT SUMMARY
Period: April 27–May 10, 1986.
Target: destroyed Unit 4.
 
Approximately 5,000 metric tons of material were dropped, including forty tons of boron compounds, 600 tons of dolomite, 1,800 tons of clay and sand, as well as lead.
 
Purpose: absorb neutrons, reduce heat generation, and isolate the central hall. The resulting layer ranges from one meter thick at the north wall to fifteen meters at the south.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Flight conditions: intense radiation, hot air, and dust above the reactor.%c[0,170,170,170]
Roof Work Permit

DECONTAMINATION WORK PERMIT
Area: roofs of Unit 3 and adjoining structures.
 
Team assignment: manually collect fragments of graphite, fuel, and structural material; throw them toward the destroyed unit.
Tools: shovel, scraper, gripping tool.
Protection: standard clothing, respirator, and additional shielding where available.
Procedure: enter on the dosimetrist's command, work only for the allotted time, return immediately at the signal.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]A second entry without authorization from the radiation-safety service is forbidden.%c[0,170,170,170]
Shelter Acceptance Certificate

STATE ACCEPTANCE COMMISSION
Date: November 30, 1986.
Facility: protective structure around Unit 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant.
 
Construction authorized by the decision of May 29, 1986. Eighteen designs were considered. The selected design combines new enclosure structures with surviving parts of the damaged unit.
 
Purpose: restrict the release of radioactive material and reduce radiation exposure. Some supporting assemblies cannot be reached for inspection; the service life of load-bearing elements requires continuous monitoring.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Commission decision: accept the Shelter facility for operation.%c[0,170,170,170]
INSAG-1/7 Comparative Memorandum

INTERNAL MEMORANDUM
Subject: revision of the assessment of the accident's causes.
 
INSAG-1, 1986: places primary emphasis on operator violations. Source information supplied by the Soviet side; no independent evidence-gathering conducted.
 
INSAG-7, 1993: confirms errors by the shift while also identifying hazardous RBMK characteristics, flaws in the shutdown rods, incomplete operating documentation, and weak state oversight.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Final assessment: responsibility extends to the operators, designers, management, and regulatory system.%c[0,170,170,170]
Three Days' Food for the Pets

TRANSCRIPT OF AN EVACUEE'S RECOLLECTION
Pripyat, April 27, 1986.
 
The radio told us to take our documents, essential belongings, and food for three days. What we heard was: we will be back soon.
 
They would not let animals onto the buses. Neighbors poured out water, left bowls of food, and locked their apartments. Dogs followed people to the boarding points. Cats watched from windows. Nobody brought cages or leashes; there would have been no room for them anyway.
 
We left without our animals because we believed there would be a return journey.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The promised three days passed. The residents were never allowed to return.%c[0,170,170,170]
Report on Abandoned Animals

ANALYTICAL BRIEF
Territory of Pripyat and the thirty-kilometer zone.
 
Conditions following the evacuation:
— pet dogs and cats remain in the city;
— livestock and domestic animals remain in rural settlements;
— animals are leaving apartments and farmyards, gathering near entrances, shops, and roads, and approaching people and vehicles.
 
Measures taken: teams have been formed to destroy abandoned animals and limit the spread of radioactive contamination beyond the resettled territory.
 
Note added to later survey materials: some of the Zone's dog population descends from pets that survived the first months after the evacuation.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The food left in the apartments was meant to last only as long as the radio had promised.%c[0,170,170,170]
Driver Kislytskyi's Record Card

ARCHIVAL PERSONNEL CARD
 
Surname: Kislytskyi.
Years of life: 1952–1986.
Employer: ATP-09123 Kyivpasazhyravtotrans.
Position: bus driver.
 
Assignment: city of Pripyat.
Date: April 27, 1986.
Duty: transport evacuees to temporary accommodation.
 
The bus convoys were assembled during the night of April 27. Vehicles were in position at boarding points by 14:00. The main transport operation ended around 17:00.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]On the city archive card, the years beside the driver's name read 1952–1986.%c[0,170,170,170]
Letter About a Missing Family

TO THE EVACUEE ACCOMMODATION AUTHORITIES
 
Please tell me where the members of my family were sent. We were assigned to different buses while boarding. The accommodation lists changed after arrival, and I was not given an exact address.
 
I have asked the executive committee and the police; neither has any information. I send notes with drivers returning to collect more people. There has still been no reply.
 
Please check the lists for every village and district that received residents of Pripyat on April 27 and inform me where my family was placed.
 
Family members: _____________________________
Place of accommodation: _____________________
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Names remain on the “family members” line. “Place of accommodation” is blank.%c[0,170,170,170]
K. Derkonis House Record

PHOTOGRAPHIC RECORD CARD
Obukhiv, May 7, 1986.
 
Location photographed: the home of K. Derkonis.
Subject: temporary accommodation of three families evacuated after the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant accident.
 
Provided by the householders:
— beds;
— clothing;
— dishes;
— food.
 
The children are housed together. The arrivals have their documents and only the personal belongings they were allowed to bring when boarding.
 
Duration of stay: ___________________________
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The “duration of stay” field was never filled in.%c[0,170,170,170]
Letter from A. V. Kuznetsov

TO THE CENTRAL COMMITTEE OF THE CPSU
M. S. Gorbachev
General Department stamp: May 15, 1986.
 
Dear Mikhail Sergeyevich,
 
By May 7, panic had begun in Kyiv. The railway stations, airport, and bus terminals were overflowing, mostly with parents and children. There were no tickets. People were abandoning work and trying to get their children out on their own.
 
The first to do so were the heads of enterprises and institutions, the city Party committee, and the Council of Ministers. They sent their own children away from Kyiv in the first days after the accident. The public saw this and followed their example.
 
I ask that the actions of these officials be investigated. I have been a Party member since 1950, but after what happened I no longer trust our leaders.
 
A. V. Kuznetsov
 
Office note: no return address. The sender could not be identified.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]“They saved their own children and abandoned ours.”%c[0,170,170,170]
Letter from L. V. Kuzmina

TO M. S. GORBACHEV
From a group of mothers in Kyiv
General Department stamp: May 28, 1986.
 
Dear Mikhail Sergeyevich,
 
Pain and desperation have driven us to write this letter. We are ready to work and help deal with the consequences of the accident, but we beg you to save our children.
 
Why have preschool and school-age children still not been evacuated from Kyiv and the Kyiv Region? Why are senior classes continuing, and why have examinations at schools and universities not been canceled?
 
Give the public dosimeters. We must know what we are feeding our children. In Moscow, people shun arrivals from Kyiv as though we were contagious, while we are told to wait calmly without information about the water, air, or food.
 
We ask you to resolve these matters immediately.
 
L. V. Kuzmina
For a group of mothers in Kyiv
 
%c[255,238,153,26]“Save our children, we beg you.”%c[0,170,170,170]
A Veteran's Letter About the Silence

TO V. V. SHCHERBITSKY
Incoming No. AN-26480, May 28, 1986.
 
Dear Vladimir Vasilyevich,
 
Every day, almost every hour, the people of Kyiv wait for clear information about conditions in the city. We trust official reports, yet those reports contradict one another.
 
On May 23, the newspaper Vechirnii Kyiv stated that all food sold through state and cooperative stores was inspected and safe. Green onions had been on sale in greengrocers throughout that time, and people were buying them.
 
On May 24, the same newspaper advised people to stop eating green onions for the time being. Who are we to believe? Is Kyiv in a hazardous zone or not? Once again, there is no direct answer.
 
We ask that the actual situation be reported to the public every day.
 
Unsigned.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The onions were already on sale when residents were advised not to eat them.%c[0,170,170,170]
Letter from the Women of Kyiv

TO THE CENTRAL COMMITTEE OF THE CPSU
From the women of the city of Kyiv
Letter dated June 12, 1986.
General Department stamp: June 24, 1986.
 
Why are we not receiving inspected food? Local strawberries, herbs, milk, and eggs are sold in the shops, yet nobody publishes the test results or permissible limits.
 
We sit behind closed windows. Our sons are working in the Zone. Our children are due to return from health retreats, and we do not know whether the water, food, or air will be safe for them.
 
We understand that a great disaster has occurred. But why are families left without clear information or assistance? At least give us food whose safety we can trust.
 
Respectfully, the women of Kyiv.
No signatures.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]“We want to scream, to weep, to plead: save us.”%c[0,170,170,170]
Letter from Vladimir Pravik

LETTER FROM MOSCOW CLINICAL HOSPITAL NO. 6
May 1986.
 
Hello, my dear Nadya and little Natasha,
 
My comrades and I have been kept at the clinic for tests. My whole watch is here, so I am not alone. We only see Moscow through the window. The doctors say no one will be discharged until the observation period is over.
 
Nadya, stay with your parents in Horodyshche for now. Once they let me go, I will come straight there. Do not cry, and take care of Natasha. I miss you both terribly.
 
Do not worry. Wait for me to come home victorious.
 
Forever yours, Volodya.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The letter promised a return. Vladimir Pravik died on May 11, 1986.%c[0,170,170,170]
Testimony of Lyudmila Ignatenko

TRANSCRIPT OF ORAL TESTIMONY
Recorded after the accident.
 
First they brought the firefighters to the Pripyat medical center. I searched for Vasily among them. Then they flew them to Moscow, to Hospital No. 6. I followed.
 
They told me not to get too close and not to touch anything. Their clothes had already been taken away. I did not tell the doctors I was pregnant. If I had, they would not have let me near him.
 
Vasily died on May 13. Later I gave birth to a girl. She lived only a few hours.
 
I never went home again.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]While Lyudmila stayed beside her husband, Pripyat was sealed and closed.%c[0,170,170,170]
Collective Letter from the Liquidators

TO THE EDITORS OF PRAVDA
Collective appeal from participants in the cleanup
Reviewed by the Central Committee of the CPSU on October 30, 1986.
 
After suffering various forms of radiation injury, our health remains poor. The housing and compensation we were promised have not been provided. Conditions at the sanatorium are unsatisfactory.
 
Doctors prescribed medicines, but they cannot be obtained. With winter approaching, we have not even been issued warm clothing. We were sent to deal with the consequences of the accident, and now each of us must prove separately where he worked and why he became ill.
 
We ask you to intervene and compel the responsible organizations to honor the promises made to us.
 
Official resolution: verify the stated facts; recognize the treatment of those affected as inexcusably callous.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]After cleaning up the disaster, people had to prove they had taken part in it.%c[0,170,170,170]
Efrem Lukatsky's Recollection

TRANSCRIPT OF EFREM LUKATSKY'S RECOLLECTIONS
Events of April–May 1986.
 
First came a metallic taste and a dry throat. Then a physicist I knew called and said it would be better to leave Kyiv. There were almost no official explanations. We listened to foreign radio and tried to send the children to relatives.
 
I found an old military dosimeter. Inside the apartment it reacted to our clothes. The readings rose especially high at the children's playground. Children were still playing there.
 
Five days after the explosion, we were sent out to the May Day demonstration.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Children kept playing where the dosimeter was already warning of danger.%c[0,170,170,170]
Petrus Household Register

EVACUEE ACCOMMODATION RECORD
Zahaltsi, June 1986.
 
Household: the Petrus family.
Temporarily accommodated:
— the Andrusenko family;
— the Hryhorenko family.
Former residence of the arrivals: Komsomolets Polissia State Farm, thirty-kilometer zone.
 
Families in the house: 3.
Dishes and household items are shared by agreement. Storage space for belongings is limited. The evacuees possess only what they were able to bring when they left.
 
End date of temporary accommodation: __________
 
%c[255,238,153,26]The word “temporary” was left without an end date.%c[0,170,170,170]
Permit to Visit Family Graves

SINGLE-ENTRY PASS TO THE EXCLUSION ZONE
Memorial week, 1989.
 
Full name: ___________________________________
Former place of residence: ___________________
 
Purpose of entry: visit the burial place of relatives.
 
Permitted:
— travel only along the approved route;
— brief presence on cemetery grounds;
— entry and departure as part of a registered group.
 
Forbidden:
— unauthorized visits to residential homes;
— deviation from the route;
— removal of personal belongings, food, or household goods without radiometric inspection.
 
Departure recorded: __________________________
 
%c[255,238,153,26]They were allowed to visit the graves before they were allowed to visit their own homes.%c[0,170,170,170]
Personal Belongings Disposal Record

CONTAMINATED PROPERTY REGISTER
Kyiv Region, 1987–1988.
 
The disposal site receives property belonging to residents of resettled communities: clothing, household goods, furniture, and other items that cannot be returned without radiometric inspection.
 
Items within permissible levels are to be cleaned or stored. Anything contaminated above the established limits is to be isolated. Owners may not retrieve property without authorization.
 
The inventory retains only ordinary descriptions — coat, child's bed, suitcase, dishes. The owners' surnames are often missing.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Everything people had hoped to collect after three days became the contents of a disposal site.%c[0,170,170,170]
Shpakovych Family Record

PHOTO ARCHIVE. ACCOMPANYING RECORD
Marianivka, Narodychi District.
Photographed: July 1990.
 
Subject: the Shpakovych family.
Event: final resettlement from an affected community.
 
The family is identified as the village's last permanent household. The photograph shows their belongings loaded for removal; the house and outbuildings are left behind.
 
Time between the accident and resettlement: four years.
Permanent residents after the family departs: none.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]When the Shpakovych family left, the village had no permanent residents remaining.%c[0,170,170,170]
Undeveloped Film from Pripyat

PHOTOGRAPHIC MATERIAL RECORD
 
Medium: Svema negative film.
Frames: 36.
Photographer: Alexander, construction worker.
Location: the city of Pripyat.
Date: before February 1986.
 
The owner left the film in his apartment before departing for work in Yakutia. It was recovered during a visit to the city roughly a year later. By then the apartment had been looted, but the packet of film remained on top of a wardrobe.
 
The film was developed and printed several decades later.
Contents: the streets, homes, and daily life of Pripyat before the evacuation.
 
%c[255,238,153,26]Thirty-six frames of a city whose residents still expected to come home.%c[0,170,170,170]
